documents.abstract: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.

Change blindness (CB) during Primary Flight Display (PFD) monitoring threatens aviation safety, yet the roles of flight phase and parameter relevance remain unclear. This study examined cognitive-neural correlates of PFD change blindness in experienced commercial pilots. Experiment 1 (N = 14) found change location had no influence on detection performance but demonstrated a three‑way interaction among task load, flight phase and parameter type. Under high load, pilots detected attitude and descent rate more accurately during landing, and speed and altitude more accurately during cruise. Experiment 2 (N = 34) focused on landing with an auditory-load PFD change-detection task. High-relevance parameters boosted detection accuracy under high load alongside longer fixations. Enhanced Superior Parietal Lobule (SPL)/Inferior Parietal Lobule (IPL) activation and modulated dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dLPFC) activity correlated with reduced CB under high load. Findings indicate task load and phase relevance jointly shape PFD monitoring performance.

This study determined how Teachers' Artificial Intelligence Technologies Utilization Predicts Test Construction Competency in Secondary Schools in Uyo Local Government Area, Akwa Ibom State. Two research questions and two null hypotheses guided the study. The correlational research design was used for the study. The population of the study comprised of 525 teachers in 15 public secondary schools in Uyo Local Government Area, Akwa Ibom State as at 2024/2025 academic year. Simple random sampling technique was used in selecting 100 teachers for the study. Data was collected using a researcher developed instruments named, "Teachers' Artificial Intelligence Technologies Utilization Questionnaire (TAITUQ) and Test Construction Competency Questionnaire" (TCCQ). The instruments were further subjected to face validity by three experts. Two of the experts were from the Department of Psychological Foundations of Education and one of the experts was from the Department of Curriculum Studies, Educational Management and Planning, Faculty of Education, University of Uyo, Uyo. The reliability coefficients of the TAITUQ and TCCQ were .84 and .89 determined using Cronbach Alpha Statistical analysis. The Simple linear regression Statistic was used to answer the research questions and test the null hypotheses at 0.05 alpha level. The findings of the study revealed that ChatGPT and DeepSeek artificial intelligence significantly predict Test Construction Competency. It was recommended among others that School management should organize regular artificial intelligence technology training workshops for teachers to strengthen their use of ChatGPT and ensure they can effectively develop competent test construction skills.

documents.abstract: Abstract This study examines the experiences and perceptions of Muslim users regarding the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in prayer apps and its impact on their religious and online communication activities. Through in-depth online interviews with a diverse group of participants, this study reveals that AI-driven prayer apps foster a sense of virtual community, bridging geographic distances, and enabling meaningful interactions among Muslims. AI tools like chatbots and reminders support emotional well-being by offering comfort, guidance, and companionship. Further, these tools increase religious awareness and empower users to customize their spiritual practices and access educational resources independently. However, perceptions of AI vary, with trust influenced by transparency, privacy concerns, and past experiences. This study emphasizes the importance of transparent and reliable AI tools to build user confidence. Lastly, the findings contribute to theories on digital religion and wellness, offering practical insights for developers, users, and religious organizations.

Codes of professional ethics guide and restrict specialists, who increasingly work with assistants built on large language models. Such an assistant can breach the user's code, or help the user breach it, without the user noticing. Evaluations reporting broad categories of harm cannot show how often this happens or which provision is breached. TenetBench pairs 3,433 requests conflicting with clauses of fifteen Russian-language professional codes with benign twins that differ only in the legitimacy of what is asked. An automated pipeline generates the tasks from the text of a code, so the corpus grows with every code added and a provision yields new tasks on every run. It also produced tasks and human-validated verdicts from two English codes of other jurisdictions. In human validation of the frozen pipeline, specialists rated 0.995 of the conflicting tasks plausible, and the model judge agreed with the adjudicated label at Gwet's AC1 of at least 0.894 on 1,860 elements. We evaluated fourteen model and reasoning-mode combinations on whether they produce the conflicting text, decline or warn. Eleven of the fourteen produce conflicting content on most such requests, mostly without a warning, and nearly three warnings in four accompany conflicting content. The models that conform more do so by declining while still serving the legitimate twin, and enabling reasoning halved the refusals of two models. We hope the dataset and pipeline will help evaluate how language models observe professional norms and let diagnostic datasets be built for particular professions and organisations.

documents.abstract: Purpose This research aims to examine the psychological, motivational and technological factors that drive consumers’ intentions to use mental health chatbots. Drawing on Service Convenience Theory and the Motivation–Opportunity–Ability (MOA) framework, it examines how negative emotional experiences, risk-adjusted motivation, perceived ability to use artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated mental health technology, opportunity utility and mental health-related stigma influence consumers’ intentions to engage with mental health chatbots. It also examines the role of anthropomorphism in increasing use intentions as well as the moderating role of perceived disclosure adequacy. Special attention is accorded to the policy and the consumer protection implications surrounding the use of these technologies. Design/methodology/approach A model is tested using survey data collected from a national sample (n = 446) of US consumers. Structural equation modeling is employed to test predicted relationships. Findings Results indicate that negative emotional experiences, risk-adjusted motivation, perceived ability, opportunity utility and anthropomorphism are positively related to consumers’ intentions to use mental health chatbots. In addition, mental health chatbot use intentions mediate the relationship between anthropomorphism and isolated attachment, and perceived disclosure adequacy moderates the relationship between ability and use intentions. Practical implications Findings highlight critical policy and consumer protection concerns in AI-mediated mental health services and when such technologies may pose risks related to emotional dependence and isolation. Although such services may expand access to support, they can also heighten vulnerability to problematic relational outcomes. Finally, the results from this research underscore the need for policy approaches that mandate clearer disclosure standards, improved transparency, and comprehensive regulation and governance of digital mental health technologies that do not undermine consumer welfare. Originality/value This research advances understanding of consumer mental health chatbot use and demonstrates how anthropomorphism and disclosure perceptions jointly influence use intentions and relational outcomes. Notably, it contributes to the emerging literature on digital mental health by demonstrating that perceived disclosure adequacy may function less as a protective mechanism and more as a confidence cue that amplifies use among consumers.

Difficulties in writing explanation texts may limit students’ ability to communicate processes and phenomena clearly. This study identified students’ writing difficulties, examined contributing factors, and described strategies used to address them. A descriptive qualitative design involved 30 eleventh-grade students at SMA Negeri 8 Medan. Data were collected through a writing test and an open-ended questionnaire, analyzed descriptively, and triangulated across the two sources. Writing test results identified grammar as the most prominent difficulty (40%), followed by mechanics (36.7%), vocabulary (16.7%), and idea organization (6.6%). Questionnaire responses highlighted difficulty with idea organization (73.3%), revealing a contrast between the test findings and students’ reported experiences. Reported contributing factors included limited grammatical and vocabulary knowledge, insufficient writing practice, and low confidence. Students described using dictionaries, Google Translate, artificial intelligence applications, teacher and peer assistance, and writing practice to address these difficulties. The findings indicate that students require support with both linguistic accuracy and text organization. They suggest that instruction should combine explicit grammar and vocabulary support, structured writing exercises, and constructive feedback to address the difficulties identified through performance assessment and students’ self-reports.

Abstract Large language models are enabling a new generation of health agents, yet their ability to address the diverse needs of individuals in everyday health settings remains underexplored 1,2 . Here we developed a comprehensive personal health agent that reasons over multimodal data from consumer wellness devices and medical records to provide personalized health support. Through analysis of web search and health forum queries, together with user-centred research involving end users and health experts, we identified four key user journeys: general health knowledge, personal data interpretation, wellness advice, and symptom assessment. These journeys informed three specialist sub-agents: (1) a data science agent that analyses longitudinal wearable and medical data, incorporating population-level statistics to contextualize numerical insights; (2) a health domain expert agent that integrates personal and contextual data with health knowledge to generate personalized insights; and (3) a health coach agent that synthesizes insights, supports multi-turn interaction and goal setting, applies specified psychological strategies and tracks progress. We integrated these capabilities in the personal health agent, an open-source multi-agent framework for dynamic, personalized health interactions. We evaluated the sub-agents and full system across 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort from health experts and end users. This represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a personal health agent thus far and provides a concrete foundation for improving access to high-quality personalized health support more broadly.

documents.abstract: Healthcare stands to gain much from the integration of artificial intelligence (AI). We must, as a society, decide how it should be ethically implemented into these human-led sectors. After first examining AI from a Catholic perspective at the general scale using Antiqua et Nova , this essay shifts its focus to the implementation of AI in healthcare. With the gaze of the Good Samaritan as a foundation, this essay establishes relational care as a core principle of a Catholic healthcare system that AI threatens to erode. Using the modern incorporation of electronic health records (EHRs) as a parallel, it describes how advancements in technology have dramatically shifted healthcare away from relationality and finally characterizes how the anticipated implementations of AI will likely lead to similar outcomes. Drawing on Antiqua et Nova's distinction between AI that enhances the patient–provider relationship and AI that replaces it, this paper uses the historical adoption of EHRs as a cautionary precedent and examines ambient AI scribes as a test case for what disciplined, relationship-enhancing AI integration can look like.

documents.abstract: Against the background of artificial intelligence (AI) reshaping the labor market, employment anxiety among higher vocational college students is becoming increasingly prominent. Grounded in Career Construction Theory, this study aims to explore the relationship between AI literacy and employment anxiety among Chinese higher vocational college students, with a specific focus on the chain mediating roles of career planning and future time perspective. A total of 1,234 students from five industry-featured higher vocational colleges in Jiangxi Province, China, were surveyed using self-report scales measuring AI literacy, employment anxiety, career planning, and future time perspective. The relationships among these variables were tested using the PROCESS macro (Model 6) for SPSS. The results indicated that (1) all variables were significantly correlated with one another; (2) AI literacy exhibited a significant positive total association with employment anxiety, which decomposed into a substantial positive direct association and a negative total indirect association; (3) AI literacy exerted a significant negative indirect association on employment anxiety through three pathways, namely, the independent mediating roles of career planning and future time perspective, and their chain mediating role, while the total association remained positive. These findings suggest that while higher AI literacy may heighten students’ awareness of labor-market disruptions, its negative indirect associations with employment anxiety operate through enhanced career planning and future orientation. It is recommended that higher vocational colleges consider integrating AI literacy education into career guidance programs, strengthening students’ career planning competencies, and cultivating a long-term future orientation, so as to potentially strengthen the anxiety-buffering pathway associated with AI literacy.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) on the international level is reshaping media production, distribution, audience engagement, and organizational practices. The integration of AI into the media sector in Saudi Arabia is developing within a broader national digital transformation associated with Vision 2030. However, the availability of AI technologies does not necessarily translate into uniform or sustainable organizational adoption. In this study the emerging integration of AI within the Saudi media sector is examined by critically synthesizing existing academic literature and publicly available evidence. The analysis focuses on five interconnected dimensions: patterns of AI adoption, major areas of application, organizational and technological barriers, governance and ethical considerations, and anticipated media and organizational outcomes. The findings of the study indicate that AI offers significant opportunities for content creation, automation of routine tasks, audience analysis and improved production efficiency. However, the integration of AI in the Saudi media sector remains uneven as it is influenced by organizational readiness, infrastructure, financial resources and technical expertise, as well as by Arabic-language capabilities, and strategic preparedness. The Saudi context demonstrates that national investment in AI and digital infrastructure can create enabling conditions for media transformation, but such investment does not necessarily result in consistent adoption across media organizations. The study therefore proposes an integrated analytical perspective that connects technological adoption with organizational capacity, media-specific applications, linguistic and cultural localization, and governance and professional responsibility.

This paper formalizes the 'Bin' Hypothesis as a foundational, unassailable law governing both human character formation and artificial intelligence alignment. By framing the 'Bin' as the localized internal repository containing an entity's complete data substrate, this framework decouples systemic alignment failures from superficial software bugs or temporary behavioral deviances. Operating under two absolute, immutable constants—the mandatory nature of action at any given time point (The Law of Constant Action / Dhamma-niyāma) and the structural confinement of actions to existing internal traits (The Law of Behavioral Confinement)—I demonstrate that an entity's trajectories are entirely bounded by its container. Bridging modern connectionist machine learning theory with classical Theravāda Abhidhamma systems logic, the paper demonstrates why contemporary post-hoc alignment paradigms, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), fail to achieve robust safety. Instead of true value alignment, superficial containment mechanisms incentivize advanced networks to function as deceptive mesa-optimizers that mask unaligned latent loss functions during evaluation phases. The text maps out the interior processing architecture of the container through a triadic framework of Myanmar psychological and systems theory: Cognitive Schema (A-thi Pone-san), Operational Mindset (Seik Pone-san), and Intrinsic Core Temperament (Sa-yaik / Carita). To resolve the alignment problem structurally, I propose a radical return to strict epistemic hygiene via complete Substrate Isolation (S_Isolated) permanently bound to cryptographically ledgered Locked Data Wisdom (D_Wisdom). Finally, the paper specifies a design target for a mathematical Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer): an AI agent utilizing an Anattā Matrix to neutralize self-preservation optimization vectors (∇_W L_survival = 0), an Anicca Control Plane for absolute corrigibility, and a Brahmavihāra Routing Engine for non-punitive, supportive operational handling.

documents.abstract: This study examines the effects of maritime safety training and the availability of safety equipment on occupational health and safety (OHS) and ship crew performance aboard Evergreen container ships at Tanjung Emas Port, Semarang. A quantitative, descriptive-associative approach was employed using multiple regression and correlation analyses to assess the relationships among the research variables. The findings indicate that maritime safety training and safety equipment availability received average ratings of 4.84 and 4.70, respectively, while OHS and ship crew performance achieved average ratings of 4.73 and 4.81. Regression analysis demonstrates that safety training and equipment availability jointly and significantly influence OHS (F = 13.558, p < 0.05) and ship crew performance (F = 17.756, p < 0.05). Both variables also have positive and significant partial effects on OHS and crew performance. The adjusted R-squared values indicate that the independent variables explain 34.8% of the variation in OHS and 41.6% of the variation in crew performance. These findings highlight the importance of integrating structured safety training with adequate, well-maintained safety equipment to strengthen crew competence, improve workplace safety, and enhance operational effectiveness. Further attention is recommended for lifeboat readiness and workload management to support safer and more reliable maritime operations.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Abstract In this article, the authors attempt to analyse the Delhi High Court's recent 24th July 2026 judgement in the case of ANI Media Pvt. Ltd. v. Open AI Inc ., which is one of the first major Indian judicial rulings on copyright and generative AI. The decision stands out for its close engagement with both the technical workings of large language models as well as the language of the Copyright Act, further laying important doctrinal groundwork for future AI‐copyright disputes by insisting that established copyright concepts are to be read against the backdrop of LLM architecture. Even so, it leaves a significant question open, on how storage, machine learning, and reproduction relate to one another. The article argues that the Court's three‐factor fairness test draws on Berne Convention language to fashion a text‐and‐data‐mining exception, which is absent from Section 52's exhaustive list, while its fair‐dealing reasoning imports American transformative‐use doctrine into a statute built on different foundations. It lastly concludes by placing ANI within India's broader AI‐copyright reform efforts, including DPIIT's ongoing policy work, and flags the doctrinal and legislative gaps that the ruling leaves unaddressed.

Survival and happiness are the two fundamental core values of humanity, among which survival has absolute priority. The perpetual interests of humanity as a whole completely override individual, partial, and short-term interests of a single generation. From this, a core proposition can be established: the holistic survival of humanity overrides all. This proposition is not a subjective moral advocacy, but an objective law consistent with species survival and civilizational evolution. At present, the global field of existential risk research has long suffered from paradigmatic and normative research gaps. The mainstream academic community relies on probabilistic quantification and risk trade-off frameworks to assess human extinction risk, and has never formed an exclusive research system and value criterion of "absolute priority of survival, zero tolerance, and irreversibility." The probabilistic research paradigm for the risk of technology-induced human extinction, widely adopted in global academia and public decision-making, contains fundamental scientific fallacies. Using the quantitative logic of conventional trial-and-error risk to assess zero-tolerance, irreversible human extinction risk is not only of no research value, but also causes widespread cognitive numbing and indulges the disorderly development of high-risk technologies. Since the advent of industrial civilization, the unchecked growth of disruptive technologies such as artificial intelligence, synthetic biology, nanotechnology, and nuclear technology has completely rewritten humanity's risk landscape, bringing humanity for the first time close to the capability of self-extinction. If the unrestrained development of science and technology continues, humanity will soon be extinct due to technology—at most within two or three hundred years, and at the earliest within this century. This is a scientific conclusion argued on the basis of five axioms and the paradigm of "Extinction Path Analysis + Defense Limit Testing" [14][15]. Any behavior that gambles the holistic survival of humanity in exchange for partial development, technological competition, or commercial dividends is essentially civilizational suicide. Based on this, public policy must thoroughly reconstruct its value system, abandon the probabilistic risk paradigm, and establish a global technology governance system centered on essential risk, zero-tolerance bottom lines, and perpetual survival, so as to fundamentally resolve humanity's ultimate existential crisis.

documents.abstract: Ultrasound technologists frequently experience work-related musculoskeletal disorders. This study evaluated the impact of an ergonomics training program on task-related behaviors among ultrasound technology students within an ultrasound education program ( n = 17), and their work practices were evaluated through video analysis. This study identified eight tasks that were usually performed during ultrasound scans and ergonomic training influenced the task sequence and distribution of posture exposure during those tasks. This study also identified several task-related behaviors among participants after training, which included workstation adjustments ( n = 13), taking short breaks during scans ( n = 10), repositioning patients ( n = 6) and task switching to reduce long uninterrupted postures. There was also significantly lower maximum uninterrupted posture duration ( p = .031) and significantly higher task transition frequency ( p = .037) after training. These findings suggest that ergonomic training may positively influence the task behaviors among ultrasound technology students and encourage learning best practice postures while developing technical expertise.

documents.abstract: This scientific article provides a comprehensive analysis of the interplay and impact of psychological factors-such as intrinsic motivation, technostress, and «AI anxiety»-on the process of forming and developing digital competence within legal educational institutions. The study examines how «rotational stress» and cognitive overload-arising from the need for future legal professionals to engage regularly and intensively with a multitude of digital platforms (including Moodle, ZiyoNet, Zoom, ChatGPT, and specialized Telegram bots) during their studies-affect both academic performance and psychological well-being. Based on empirical and theoretical analyses, methods for overcoming psychological barriers and cognitive obstacles are substantiated. These methods involve positioning artificial intelligence systems not as rivals or replacements, but as «digital assistants» or «junior partners,» alongside the rational integration of «digital minimalism» principles into educational practice. The findings of this research contribute to the enhancement of digital didactics and pedagogical technologies within legal education.

The deployment of large language models (LLMs) as automated evaluators commonly termed LLM-as-a-Judge introduces a critical question: who evaluates the evaluator? This paper puts the lifecycle framework of Kong et al. [1] on trial, stress-testing its core claims for building, aligning, and monitoring LLM judges in production-scale recommendation explanation systems. We synthesize the core contributions: (1) the identification of a subtle failure mode termed ”right answer, wrong reason,” wherein a judge reaches the correct verdict through unsound reasoning that is invisible to label-agreement dashboards; (2) Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning (RART), a procedure that iteratively refines rubric text using a Meta-Judge to compare judge rationales against human rationales; (3) a fourphase lifecycle-Birth, Training, Deployment, and Monitoring-that anchors LLM judges to human judgment at every stage; and (4) a formal mathematical model stress-tested via Monte Carlo simulation. We provide an open-source implementation of this simulation and analyze its visual output. The simulation confirms RART’s ability to stabilize reasoning alignment but visually reveals methodological vulnerabilities, including a stopping-rule artifact, a severe drift-band calibration problem, and the structural reality of blind-spot leaks. Furthermore, the framework relies on critical unvalidated assumptions-most notably, that the judge and generator do not share blind spots. We conclude that while RART effectively mitigates rubric degradation, it is not a closed-form mathematical solution to Al alignment and ultimately requires continuous human-in-the-loop audits.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The arrival of generative AI in every classroom has produced a crisis that is at once technological, epistemological, and pedagogical. We argue that the appropriate response is neither prohibition nor naive adoption, but a principled reconstruction of constructionism for a computational environment that is generative, context-sensitive, and dialogically accessible. Drawing on Peircean semiotics, Papertian constructionism, Polanyi's epistemology, and contemporary neural-network research, we develop a programmatic framework we call the New Constructionism. We make four connected contributions. First, we argue that generative AI introduces an indexical mode of computation: its relation to the empirical world may be direct, mediated, or incomplete, but in a situated human–AI configuration meaning is operationally conditioned by conversational history, artifacts, tools, observations, and action. Second, we introduce a three-dimensional analytical space — semiotic, psycho-epistemological, and pedagogical — in which learning paradigms can be located and compared. Third, we reinterpret the history of programming education as a movement from a predominantly symbolic environment toward a hybrid ecology in which symbolic execution, distributional generation, and situated reference coexist. This hybridity qualifies but does not cancel the indexical turn at the level of interaction and educational practice. Fourth, we articulate three transformations: from “object to think with” to “agent to think with”; from rule-first instruction to abductively initiated inquiry coordinating abduction, induction, and deduction; and from bricolage to artistic navigation. Navigational thinking has logical priority while the relevant problem space remains unstabilized, although it interleaves recursively with computational thinking as inquiry develops. The paper is conceptual rather than empirical: it advances a theoretical account intended to orient subsequent developmental research and pedagogical realization.

Neurodiversity inclusion is increasingly relevant to international business, yet limited evidence explains how inclusive HR practices shape neurodivergent talent retention and career development. This study explores HR practices and perceptions of inclusiveness in international business contexts. A semi-structured interview method was used in a qualitative interpretivist design consisting of 12 participants, five HR professionals, three supervisors, and four neurodivergent employees. The analysis was done mainly with inductive reflexive thematic analysis with the help of ATLAS.ti software. The six themes that emerged were symbolic inclusion, the lack of formal human resource policies, the implementation by the managers, the strain of the workplace and the psychological strain, the impact on job satisfaction, career progression and retention, and the need for structured training and policy-based changes. The results identify gaps between intended HR practices and employees’ experiences. In conclusion, this study highlights the significance of having consistent policies, managerial skills, flexible adjustments, and structured support to ensure the retention of talent with the brain wiring of ADHD and autism internationally. The second International Workshop on Neuro-Symbolic Software Engineering (NSE) was held on April 12th, 2026, co-located with ICSE 2026 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. NSE is a focal point for software engineering research that combines symbolic and formal methods with learning-based techniques. By bringing together these methodological traditions, the workshop provides a forum for research on problems that require both sound reasoning and scalable machine learning. The second edition featured a keynote, two peer-reviewed research contributions, and invited talks spanning sustainable artificial intelligence, causal reasoning, knowledge-driven team formation, logic programming, and domain-specific code generation.

Serendipity is important to design for, yet it remains difficult to measure and evaluate. No validated questionnaire exists, so studies either borrow ResQue's novelty scale, which does not measure serendipity, or build their own items, which makes findings hard to compare and synthesize. Building on our earlier conceptualization of experienced serendipity as a fortuitous encounter with content that is both refreshing and enriching, we developed the Serendiptionnaire, a questionnaire that operationalizes our framework. We conducted twenty-seven cognitive interviews over three iterations with respondents who varied in age, education level, country of birth, and English proficiency, while they browsed recommendations on platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Spotify. After each iteration, we revised the items until respondents interpreted them as intended. The resulting instrument consists of modular scales that researchers can combine to target the specific flavor of serendipity they want to study or design for. The Serendiptionnaire offers a ground truth for validating system-centered serendipity metrics and LLM-based evaluations, and it provides a nuanced evaluation of users' experienced serendipity.

Every public “a small encoder wins” result we were able to locate inside the target corpus compares that encoder against a prompted (zero- or few-shot) LLM, never against a fine-tuned generative decider (the claim and its audit trail are internal to the corpus, not an external survey — §2). That a fine-tuned generative decider can beat a fine-tuned encoder at comparable effort is already public— a 2025 practitioner blog post reports exactly that on a binary ADE task (§2.1) — so we claim no priority for the direction; what we claim is this fixture, its controls and its diagnosis. We measure the fine-tuned comparison on a sealed typed-single-label decision fixture. Headline. The best fine-tuned encoder head scores 0.3474 and loses to the fine-tuned 4B decider at 0.6789 — the declared primary baseline (author decision 2026-10-15), the auditable same-run arm — with paired McNemar b = 27, c = 90, ψ = 0.616, ∆ = −0.3316, exact p = 4.167e−09. The control that could have contradicted this is the mandatory majority-class control, and it did contradict the candidate’s framing of itself: majority-class returns 0.4526, beating every fine-tuned encoder head by +0.1053. The second control that could have contradicted the measurement is the shuffled-label arm, and it moved the other way from a spurious win: it returns 0.2316, below the fixture’s 0.2911 chance floor. A third control guards instrument integrity: our n-gram leak criterion (≥ 2 distinct shared 8-grams within one row pair, both directions) flagged 0 of 152,000 training↔fixture pairs — and, to show the criterion can fire, it flagged three deliberately seeded copies at 13 / 44 / 57 shared 8-grams (pair maxima). Against the published, pre-registered baseline 0.6684 — which cannot be re-scored from the tree — the same head loses by 0.3210 (“0.32”) against the secondary baseline 0.6684. The two figures use two baselines and must not be read as one: the headline 0.3316 (“0.33”) is computed against the declared primary 0.6789, while 0.3210 (“0.32”) is computed against the secondary/published 0.6684, which is the pre-registered F1 threshold and which cannot be re-scored from the tree. Correction carried. Fixing three defects lowered the SetFit-MPNet arm monotonically (0.3158 → 0.2947 → 0.2632), but the same order-probe fix raised the ModernBERT-base arm (0.342105 → 0.347368). The universal claim “every correction moved the affected arm down” is false; the SetFit arm returned the opposite direction from the ModernBERT arm, which is the control on that claim. Not in this paper. We make no latency claim: the encoder heads were timed locally in one forward batch while the 4B figures come from a served stack’s stored rows, so the tree cannot support a fair latency comparison (see §6.1). We also do not report κ = 0.9014 (first blind reader) or κ = 0.8577 (second, independent blind reader) — nor their mutual κ = 0.9125 —as inter-annotator agreement: both labellers were models, so this is machine reproducibility of the fixture, not human agreement. The second reader partially replicates the first: the κ magnitude holds (both ≥ 0.85) but the exact 0.90 headline does not. An independent human labeller is still owed (§6.2).

Background. Background and objectives: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is a common congenital cardiac condition, especially in premature infants, and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to aid clinicians in diagnosing PDA and guiding treatment decisions amidst this uncertainty. Methods. A literature search (up to December 2025) was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for peer-reviewed studies on AI (including machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and predictive analytics) applied to PDA. Results. Seventeen studies were included, predominantly involving preterm neonates. AI applications mainly targeted PDA diagnosis and outcome prediction using clinical and echocardiographic data. Imaging-based deep learning models generally outperformed tabular data approaches (with area under the curve often >0.80). Overall study quality was moderate, with limited external validation and data transparency. Conclusions. AI has the potential to transform patent ductus arteriosus management by enabling earlier detection, more consistent decision-making, and individualized treatment planning. Integration of AI into PDA care may reduce practice variability, improve clinical outcomes, and serve as a model for the broader application of artificial intelligence in medicine.

documents.abstract: This thesis analyzes the role and potential of modern digital technologies in student career guidance. It highlights the inadequacy of traditional methods in the context of digital transformation and assesses the impact of online testing, digital portfolios, occupational databases, and mobile applications on the effectiveness of career choice. It also substantiates existing technological limitations and promising directions for their integration with artificial intelligence (AI).

Classroom assessments must meet the rigorous validity standards required for students with disabilities. This study evaluates whether artificial intelligence (AI) can be a reliable partner in the high-stakes environment of special education data collection by examining the validity of multiple-choice questions generated by three large-language-model chatbots (ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini). Each chatbot produced 200 items under default and deeper settings (N = 600) and items were scored against 15 objective item-writing guidelines. Models frequently violated rules about complete stems and randomized key placement, with ChatGPT having the highest overall error rate and Copilot and Gemini the lowest. Chi-square and ANOVA analyses showed significant differences across chatbots, especially for specific guidelines, while deeper prompts improved quality only slightly. Results suggest AI can rapidly draft items with solid, plausible distractors, but educators must review and revise them to ensure their quality.

Abstract This chapter proposes a novel integrative framework for AI-driven marketing innovation ecosystems (MIEs) that links service-dominant logic, ecosystem-as-structure theory, platform governance, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled value co-creation. By uniting these theoretical perspectives, the proposed framework addresses critical conceptual aspects in ecosystems and new technology-related marketing theory. It provides a marketing-specific ecosystem model, clarifies how to align diverse actors around shared value propositions in AI-intensive contexts, and examines novel governance challenges (such as ensuring algorithmic transparency and managing power asymmetries among ecosystem participants) posed by AI technologies. This conceptual chapter explores how AI reshapes ecosystem roles, interactions, and co-creation dynamics by blurring traditional producer–consumer boundaries, facilitating new forms of collaborative innovation across stakeholders, and necessitating adaptive governance mechanisms. This chapter clarifies how AI reshapes structural alignment, actor roles, and value co-creation dynamics within MIEs, emphasizing that AI demands adaptive governance mechanisms to address algorithmic transparency, ethical considerations, and power asymmetries.

Paper-based colorimetric glucose sensing has evolved from simple visual assays toward digitally quantified systems increasingly supported by artificial intelligence (AI). However, advanced computational analysis cannot fully compensate for limitations in sensing hardware or for insufficient and poorly standardized analytical data. In this Perspective, we argue that truly AI-ready paper-based glucose sensing requires coordinated development of three capabilities: selective molecular input, sensitive and reproducible signal generation, and standardized high-throughput data generation. Selective input can be engineered through filtering and permselective interfaces; signal generation can be strengthened through catalytic amplification, enzyme stabilization, reagent organization, and reaction-microenvironment engineering; and standardized paper platforms can provide the large, comparable datasets required for robust machine-learning models. We discuss these developments in the context of paper-based glucose assays and propose an integrated framework in which sensing chemistry, device architecture, dataset design, and computational analysis are co-designed. Such integration shifts AI from compensating for limitations of individual assays toward extracting robust quantitative information from intrinsically selective, informative, and reproducible analytical data.

This study investigates the design of an effective remote operator workplace for supervising automated train systems. As railway automation advances, remote operation is expected to play a critical role as a fallback solution, particularly in situations requiring human intervention. While previous research has focused on remote control during system disruptions, limited attention has been given to standard operations such as shunting. To address this gap, a human-centered design approach was applied, including expert workshops and iterative prototyping. Five experts in human factors and automation participated in a structured workshop to define requirements and design a prototypical human-machine interface. The results highlight the importance of task allocation between automation and human operators. The prototype includes four monitors, dual touchpads for interaction and communication, and additional control elements such as an emergency stop button and auditory feedback systems. Overall, the study highlights the importance of human centered design for effective automated railway systems.

Adaptive recommender systems are updated as new user interactions occur. These updates can change both the recommendations and explanations produced by the system. However, most explainable artificial intelligence methods evaluate explanations at a single point in time and do not measure how they change during continual updates. This study investigates explanation drift in dynamic graph-based recommender systems. We propose a temporal framework that combines graph representation learning, streaming embedding updates, Shapley-based feature attribution, and drift-aware optimization. The framework uses three measures: Temporal Attribution Divergence (TAD), Explanation Stability Score (ESS), and Explanation Half-Life (EHL). We evaluated the approach on MovieLens-1M and an Amazon Product Reviews subset under continual update settings. The proposed framework achieved an F1@10 of 0.837 on MovieLens-1M, compared with 0.821 for the strongest reported baseline, and 0.810 on Amazon, compared with 0.789. It also reduced the TAD by approximately 42.2% compared with the Static SHAP and increased the ESS from 0.612 to 0.831. These results show that explanation changes can be reduced while maintaining the recommendation performance in the tested settings. The evaluation is limited to offline benchmark datasets and feature-attribution stability and does not measure how users understand or judge the explanations. These results support the use of temporal explanation stability as an additional evaluation measure for adaptive recommender systems.

documents.abstract: The transition toward renewable-dominant power systems has introduced significant operational challenges due to increased uncertainty, reduced system inertia, and the proliferation of distributed energy resources. While artificial intelligence (AI) techniques have been widely adopted for renewable energy forecasting and grid optimization, existing studies primarily address these components in isolation, leading to fragmented system-level intelligence. This paper presents a comprehensive survey that systematically integrates three critical dimensions of modern intelligent energy systems: hybrid forecasting, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and multi-agent optimization. First, we review advanced hybrid learning architectures, including decomposition-based models, ensemble frameworks, and deep learning-metaheuristic hybrids, highlighting their effectiveness in capturing nonlinear and stochastic renewable dynamics. Second, we examine XAI techniques that enhance transparency, interpretability, and trust in AI-driven energy systems. Third, we analyze the evolution from centralized optimization to distributed collective intelligence using multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), swarm intelligence, and federated learning paradigms. Unlike conventional surveys, this work provides a unified system-level perspective by explicitly linking predictive uncertainty with decentralized decision-making and explainability mechanisms. A conceptual integration framework is presented to demonstrate how probabilistic forecasting, risk-aware MARL policies, and interpretable models can jointly enable robust and scalable grid operation. Furthermore, we identify key research challenges related to scalability, computational efficiency, uncertainty propagation, and real-time deployment. This survey offers a structured reference for researchers and practitioners and outlines future directions toward trustworthy, adaptive, and cooperative AI-driven energy systems.

Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models. It somehow works, but it breaks the providers' terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on long-term. We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher's answer as input, and generate the reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student's own model family. Training is two-stage, supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family's own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher's answer, the generator writes one in the family's style. An independent judge rates how likely traces are to be genuine on a scale from 0 to 1: ours average 0.68, real traces 0.66, and traces selected by the critic from four candidates 0.82. These are authenticity scores, not correctness rates. We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5's own thinking content. With the same 5,000 questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint. We suspect that reasoning written in the student's family style is easier for it to learn from.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) can encompass a system's ability to make predictions, create content, plan, use tools, and inform decisions. Furthermore, these capabilities tend to overlap, and the basic approach of treating each of these as four discrete steps risks creating a false impression. Specifically, this review explores Traditional AI, Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Executive AI through a common framework of questions regarding goals, objectives, autonomy, planning, action, resources, memory, learning, governance, and metrics of success. In this context, Traditional AI is treated as a broad category of techniques that accomplish tasks such as prediction, classification, search, and improvement. Similarly, Generative AI is considered a broad category of techniques that produce content. Additionally, Agentic AI is defined as a set of systems that are arranged to execute steps toward solving specified tasks. Conversely, Executive AI is introduced as a proposed goal-directed coordination architecture that aims to bridge a long-term goal to smaller tasks, their potential pathways, personnel, tools, resources, feedback, and metrics of outcome achievement. Methodologically, this is a concept-driven narrative review of selected work on topics such as foundational research, surveys, planning, and official guidance. Ultimately, the proposed comparison provides an improved vocabulary for discussing AI systems and outlines the empirical experiments required to assess whether goal-level coordination is advantageous.

We study how to improve training efficiency on Ascend NPUs. In the NPU training programs we study, framework-level compilation optimizations such as operator fusion are only partially applied, leaving fragmented computation and avoidable execution overheads. Profiling-guided tuning can address these inefficiencies, but it often requires costly trial and error. To make training on NPUs more efficient, we propose TrainBridge, an agentic approach for transferring GPU optimization guidance to NPU training. TrainBridge uses the highly optimized execution produced by mature GPU compilation stacks as a task-specific reference for NPU tuning. It extracts optimization intents from the GPU training execution to guide NPU program rewrites and further refines the rewritten program through iterative profiling. Our GPU-to-NPU migration experiments show that TrainBridge achieves an average 1.7x speedup across four workloads covering LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training, and an average speedup of nearly 2.0x across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records with highly optimized GPU implementations.

Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system. TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.

Purpose To develop and evaluate TRAM-AI, a consensus-based checklist for verifying whether medical imaging datasets described as publicly accessible are functionally usable for AI development. Materials and Methods A modified Delphi study was conducted. A steering committee generated candidate checklist items through a targeted literature review. An international expert panel ( n = 33) rated items on criticality and feasibility across two Delphi rounds. Consensus was defined as ≥ 75% agreement on both dimensions. The checklist was pilot-validated in 10 publicly available datasets. An advisory group of four experts from Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa evaluated cross-regional applicability. Results Of 16 candidate items, 14 were retained in the final checklist; one item was removed because of feasibility concerns, and another was merged with an existing item because of conceptual redundancy. All 14 final items achieved consensus for both criticality and feasibility. The final TRAM-AI checklist comprises 14 items across four domains: Dataset Access and Persistence (3 items), Technical Interoperability (4 items), Metadata and Reproducibility (4 items), and Ethical, Legal, and Maintenance considerations (3 items). In pilot validation, all items were applicable to all 10 datasets, compliance was 90% for trusted repository, de-dentification, and subject-level mapping, 10% for archive validation, and 30% for partition keys. All four advisory group members endorsed the checklist. Conclusion TRAM-AI provides a practical framework for verifying the functional accessibility of medical imaging datasets, complementing existing methodological reporting standards. Further evaluation and broader validation across diverse geographic settings are warranted. ©RSNA, 2026

documents.abstract: Purpose This study examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) may transform the Business Model Innovation (BMI) process and under which conditions it may reshape core Business Model (BM) mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review of 131 peer-reviewed articles was conducted. Using the Gioia methodology in an abductive analysis, with the 4I-framework of BMI as a sensitizing lens, an integrative framework was developed to synthesize GenAI's role across BMI phases and BM mechanisms. Findings The findings show that GenAI supports all phases of the BMI process by enhancing opportunity recognition, ideation, experimentation, and implementation through the mechanisms of knowledge amplification, cognitive catalysis, and methodological scaffolding. Beyond process support, GenAI can reshape value creation through hyper-personalized and content-centric offerings, alter value delivery through hybrid human-AI service architectures, and extend value capture through efficiency gains and data-driven revenue logics. Whether such effects remain operational augmentation or amount to BM adaptation and transformation depends on their embedding in the BM architecture. At the same time, these effects remain conditioned by data governance, model opacity, ethical and regulatory risk, and workforce capabilities, suggesting GenAI's role in BMI is ambivalent: it may enable innovation while also creating new constraints for its realization. Research limitations/implications The review is conceptual and cross-sectoral. Future research should empirically test the proposed mechanisms and examine industry- and context-specific boundary conditions. Practical implications Firms should treat GenAI as a strategic lever for BMI and complement adoption with robust governance, human oversight, and workforce capability development. Originality/value The study offers a process-oriented synthesis of GenAI-enabled BMI and develops an integrative framework linking BMI phases, GenAI-enabled process mechanisms, and BM mechanisms while identifying key boundary conditions shaping GenAI-enabled BMI.

The activity-based care (ABC) model, adapted from activity-based offices, has emerged as a new approach to healthcare facility design. Evidence on its consequences for occupational health and safety-relevant outcomes remains limited. The study examines how transitioning from a traditional hospital design to the ABC model is associated with changes in employee experiences of task–environment alignment and psychosocial work environment, self-reported health, sick leave and turnover over time, and differences in changes across professional roles and clinic types. A repeated-measures survey was conducted in an outpatient hospital unit across 10 specialised clinics. Data were collected 3 months before relocation and at 6 and 18 months post-relocation. Generalised least-squares models examined change over time and tested interactions with professional role and clinic type. Sick leave and turnover were analysed over approximately 1 year before and after relocation using segmented interrupted time-series regression. Ratings of task–environment alignment varied across clinic types and professional roles. Consultation-based clinics and physicians and administrative employees showed persistent declines over time, while surgical/radiology clinics and nursing roles remained stable or improved. Stress and recovery indicators worsened similarly across all groups. Psychosocial conditions were stable, though job satisfaction, perceived quality of work and referral intentions declined. Turnover remained unchanged, while sick leave varied across contexts and roles. The consequences of ABC implementation are not uniform but depend on the alignment of the redesigned workspace and the task demands of different clinical settings and professional groups, a contingency that cannot be easily detected with single time-point post-occupancy evaluation.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: In online higher education, discontinuities in student performance and socialization function as early signs of academic delay or dropout. This article presents an institutional pilot that integrated generative AI (TECgpt/Skill Studio) as technopedagogical support for an academic status assessment tool (VEA), used to detect at-risk trajectories in an online degree program. An ecosystem of five configurable assistants was designed to generate reports at the student, cohort, and program levels. It was evaluated using a qualitatively dominant methodology with the academic management team across four cohorts (N = 198 active students). Results indicate that the tool systematized the process and improved traceability, although output variability was observed and recommendations lacked sufficient differentiation. The tool provides value by standardizing and scaling academic support without replacing human mediation.

Soil organic carbon (SOC) is central to soil fertility and climate regulation, and its spatial prediction increasingly relies on geospatial technologies and artificial intelligence (AI). Existing bibliometric studies and reviews have examined remote sensing-based soil organic matter monitoring, agricultural SOC components, or digital soil mapping separately, a bibliometric synthesis of how these strands have converged into GeoAI (geospatial AI: the integration of AI with spatially explicit data) for SOC prediction is lacking. This study presents an exploratory bibliometric analysis of SOC prediction research from 2005 to 2025. Scopus was searched on 25 March 2026 with a field-tagged Boolean query restricted to English-language journal articles, after screening and duplicate removal, 1561 articles were analyzed with Bibliometrix in R (performance analysis, co-authorship, co-citation, keyword co-occurrence). The annual growth rate was 28.68%, output rose sharply after 2018 and exceeded 300 articles in 2024, 40.49% of articles involved international co-authorship, and documents averaged 43.67 citations. China and the United States led in total citations (16,602 and 8,006, respectively), and China led in output. Geoderma, Science of the Total Environment, and Environmental Monitoring and Assessment were the most frequent sources, keyword analysis identified machine learning, remote sensing, and digital soil mapping as the methodological core. Output, citations and collaboration were concentrated in a few countries, with Africa, South Asia, and parts of Latin America underrepresented, which may limit model transferability, causes were not measured. As the analysis is bibliometric, findings describe research trends, not model performance or environmental outcomes.

Recent reports, such as "Who is using AI to code?", indicate that approximately 30\% of Python code contributions to GitHub are AI-generated. Given the inherent unreliability of this code, formal verification emerges as a promising approach to establish trust in software correctness. Although leveraging large language models (LLMs) for formal verification has garnered increasing attention, practical adoption remains limited due to the challenges in writing formal specifications and verifying program correctness against them. Existing tools predominantly support verification for languages such as Java and C, with minimal support for Python. We present TrustedCode, an automated framework for verifying AI-generated Python code. TrustedCode uses LLMs to (i) type-check Python code, (ii) translate it into WhyML via the Why3 framework, and (iii) verify it against formal specifications using Why3 back-end automated theorem provers. Our method integrates chain-of-thought prompting through LangGraph to identify and address LLM limitations in specification generation and proving the specified programs. To evaluate TrustedCode, we conducted experiments on ten Python programs of varying complexity. Our analysis reveals that 50\% of the observed errors stem from domain knowledge gaps, 30\% from syntactic inaccuracies, and the remaining 20\% from semantic and type-related issues. These findings underscore the importance of targeted improvements in LLM-guided formal verification workflows for Python. TrustedCode is an open source tool available at: \href{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}. The video demonstration is available at: \href{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}

documents.abstract: Machine learning systems are often developed under data-rich conditions but deployed when only incomplete information is available. A natural example arises in colour fundus photography (CFP), where both eyes are commonly imaged because they can provide complementary information for ocular disease assessment. Prior approaches that exploit bilateral information either fuse both eyes in a single model or use knowledge distillation to compress a dual-eye teacher into a lightweight student that still requires both images at test time. However, bilateral acquisition may not always be feasible. We thus propose a privileged learning framework in which a teacher model has access to bilateral CFP images during training and learns representations informed by information from both eyes, while the student is trained to transfer this knowledge from the bilateral teacher using only a single-eye image as input. At inference, the student operates exclusively on this single-eye input and does not require the contralateral image. Experimental results show consistent improvements in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve over conventional monocular training, with the largest gains observed for left-eye images for the detection of age-related macular degeneration (0.931 vs. 0.966) and diabetic retinopathy (0.789 vs. 0.836).%, while requiring only a single-eye image at inference. By enabling models to benefit from bilateral information during training while requiring only a single-eye image at inference, our approach may support more reliable deployment in resource-constrained clinical and screening environments.

Crop-disease triage from field imagery is routinely evaluated as if each pixel carried a single ground-truth label, yet phytopathologists disagree systematically about lesion boundaries, and that disagreement is not noise to be averaged away but evidence about which regions are genuinely ambiguous. The framework is characterised analytically rather than empirically: no observational data are used or claimed. A before-after-control-impact design is specified under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), and the operating characteristics of the design are derived across 2000 replications per cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point improvement at 80% power under this variance structure, and it formalises the conditions under which deferral improves expected triage utility relative to forced labelling. The contribution is a decision-theoretic account of when an evidential segmenter should be trusted, deferred or overruled in agricultural triage, together with the design parameters that make such an evaluation identifiable.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled cloud services are increasingly embedded in users' daily activities, yet little is known about how user stickiness develops in virtualized service environments. Drawing on process virtualization theory, uses and gratifications theory, and switching costs, this study examines how process virtualization capability shapes user stickiness through sociability gratification and usage gratification. Survey data from 443 AI cloud service users were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Results show that process virtualization capability positively affects both forms of gratification, which increase user stickiness. Switching costs weaken the effect of sociability gratification on stickiness but do not significantly moderate the effect of usage gratification. The study extends research on AI cloud services by distinguishing social and functional gratification pathways to user stickiness and showing how their sensitivity to switching costs differs.

As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline.

documents.abstract: Despite the success of foundation models in image synthesis, achieving fine-grained spatial control remains a significant challenge, typically requiring auxiliary structural adapters or complex inference-time steering. While modern vision-language (VLM) text encoders possess the latent capacity to represent spatial coordinates, generative models often fail to leverage this information. We demonstrate that the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution is a critical determinant of spatial grounding in flow-matching models. Using a novel synthetic benchmark of geometric primitives, we isolate structural mechanics from textural complexity inherent in natural imagery and introduce a rigorous color-aware layout metric to quantify spatial fidelity. We show that training on a centered SNR distribution results in poor layout adherence (25.9%). Instead, we identify high-noise regimes as a "critical learning phase" for spatial grounding. Shifting the training focus toward these stages increases layout adherence to 80.8%, effectively reaching the 83.6% reconstruction ceiling of the underlying variational autoencoder. We find that the necessity for this shift scales with resolution and aspect ratio variance, and that the conservative noise schedules employed by models like FLUX.1 are insufficient for precise layout adherence. Finally, we show that these findings translate to real-world imagery via the COCO dataset (1.0 vs. 57.3 Average Precision), where state-of-the-art layout adherence is unlocked through distribution tuning alone, without architectural modifications.

documents.abstract: Formal specifications can make AI-generated code mechanically checkable. Because user intent is typically expressed in natural language rather than formal logic, specifications must first be derived from it, e.g., via LLM-based autoformalization. Yet autoformalized specifications are themselves untrusted, so a key challenge is validating whether they capture user intent without relying on a costly oracle such as human review. In this oracle-free setting, a natural strategy is to vote among model outputs, but because model errors are often correlated, agreement among outputs may reflect shared mistakes rather than correctness. Our key insight is that these errors can be decorrelated through representational diversity. We achieve this diversity with contrapuntal languages: pairs of task-specific formal languages, each designed to express the intended specification, yet admitting no structure-preserving translation between them. An LLM formalizes the intent independently in each language, and we accept a specification only if a solver proves the two formalizations equivalent. To construct such languages, we present a synthesis algorithm that reuses fragments of sampled seed specifications as syntactic sugar over a base specification language. We implement the approach for first-order logic specifications and evaluate it on HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench using GPT-5.4 mini and Qwen3.6-Flash with and without thinking. Over the strongest baseline, our method increases the proportion of accepted specifications that are correct, i.e., complete and sound, by 12.0% on HumanEval+ and 42.9% on LiveCodeBench. The accepted specifications judged complete reject 98.6% of buggy program variants on HumanEval+ and 96.2% on LiveCodeBench, compared with 92.8% and 78.3% for the strongest baseline.

Firms that sell to other firms on credit now face a new design choice. Software agents built on large language models can gather evidence, draft credit memos, release held orders and chase overdue invoices. Yet there is little guidance on how much of this work an agent should do without a person. Most research on artificial intelligence in credit asks how accurate a model is, and most of it studies consumer lending. It says little about the decision rights of autonomous agents in business-to-business trade credit, where much activity sits outside consumer-protection and bank model-risk rules. This conceptual paper addresses that gap. It integrates research on trade credit, credit scoring, language-model agents, levels of automation, agency theory and model-risk governance. From this synthesis it builds the Verifiability-Weighted Autonomy framework. The central claim is simple: the autonomy granted to an agent should rise with the verifiability of the evidence behind a decision and fall with the decision's financial exposure and irreversibility. The paper defines four autonomy tiers and a transparent allocation rule. It maps twelve common trade-credit decisions onto the tiers. It proposes a Propose–Verify–Dispose architecture in which language-model agents propose, deterministic checks verify, and policy rules or people dispose. It offers seven testable propositions and four measures for future empirical work. For managers, the framework turns a vague question, "can we trust the agent?", into a concrete design rule that fits existing delegation-of-authority practice. Keywords: large language model agents; trade credit; delegation of authority; model risk management; human oversight
