documents.abstract: LLM-based verification systems repair Rust proofs by revising programs in response to Verus diagnostics. When several error types are reported, pipelines such as AutoVerus and VeruSAGE select the next repair target using a preset priority. Yet each repair changes the program and the errors that follow, so the same reported types can require different choices at different states. We present VeruSteer, which learns to select error types from the outcomes of alternative repair trajectories. It constructs repair trees offline and compares paths from the same initial program by verification success, repair rounds, and final verification progress. These comparisons supervise a selector that combines step-wise imitation with trajectory preference ranking. The selector uses self-attention over the program, verifier feedback, and earlier selections to rank the currently reported types. It replaces the default priority within a single repair trajectory, keeping the existing repair agents and adding no repair or verifier calls for selection. We evaluate VeruSteer by replaying its choices on stored AutoVerus and VeruSAGE test trees under four generation configurations. Across 1,270 test trees, VeruSteer increases verified outcomes from 185 to 194 (14.57\% to 15.28\%), gaining 12 successes and losing three for a net improvement of 0.71 percentage points. Among trees where the default fails but a recorded alternative verifies, VeruSteer succeeds on 3 of 4 AutoVerus trees and 9 of 11 VeruSAGE trees. Among trees with recorded alternatives where the default verifies, it retains success on 14 of 15 AutoVerus trees and 12 of 14 VeruSAGE trees. It also finds shorter successful trajectories and improves final progress on some trees where all recorded trajectories fail.

BackgroundVideoconferencing has become central to coordinating distributed and hybrid work, but heavy reliance on virtual meetings can produce a distinctive cognitive strain commonly referred to as videoconference (Zoom) fatigue.ObjectiveGrounded in the stressor-strain-outcome (SSO) framework and informed by cognitive ergonomics, this study examined whether socio-technical demands in videoconferencing act as stressors that increase fatigue and affect employees' work functioning.MethodsOnline self-presentation pressure, social interaction load, and cognitive absorption were conceptualized as stressors that increase cognitive and attentional demands during virtual meetings. Survey data from 383 employees across multiple industries in Taiwan were analyzed using structural equation modeling.ResultsAll three stressors were positively associated with videoconferencing fatigue, which, in turn, was positively associated with work exhaustion. The direct association between videoconferencing fatigue and perceived meeting effectiveness, an indicator of collaborative performance, was not supported, suggesting that perceived meeting functioning may be maintained despite increased strain.ConclusionsThese findings extend technostress and SSO research by demonstrating how specific features of digital collaboration technologies reshape cognitive workload and strain in modern work systems. The findings also offer practical implications for designing healthier meeting practices, supporting sustainable remote and hybrid work arrangements, and informing organizational policies on digital collaboration.

This study, titled “Virtual Frontliners: A Study on the Psychosocial Effects and Coping Mechanisms of Filipino Healthcare Virtual Assistants,” explored the lived psychosocial experiences and coping mechanisms of Filipino healthcare virtual assistants (HVAs) engaged in remote healthcare-related work. The study examined the demands associated with healthcare support work, the emotional and social effects of working remotely, the strategies participants used to manage stress, and the forms of organizational support they considered helpful. The study employed a qualitative descriptive phenomenological design. Eight Filipino healthcare virtual assistants were purposively selected based on the study criteria. Data were generated through individual semi-structured interviews conducted remotely through Zoom or Google Meet. Prior to the interview, informed consent was completed electronically through Google Forms. The interviews lasted approximately 20–30 minutes and explored participants’ work demands, psychosocial experiences, work-life boundaries, job satisfaction and motivation, coping, workplace resources, and suggested support strategies. With participant consent, the interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed for analysis. The interview transcripts were analyzed using a Colaizzi-guided descriptive phenomenological procedure. The researcher repeatedly read the complete transcripts, extracted significant statements, formulated meanings, clustered related meanings into themes, developed an exhaustive description, and synthesized the fundamental structure of the experience. Five major themes emerged: Accuracy Under Pressure; Flexibility, Boundaries, and Disconnection; Strain, Growth, and Meaning; Structured Coping and Recovery; and Resources and Support Shape Well-Being. The findings showed that the participants experienced remote HVA work as demanding but meaningful, with psychosocial well-being shaped by the balance between job demands and available personal, social, and organizational resources. The participants commonly relied on task prioritization, breaks, rest and sleep, family time, deliberate work-life boundaries, and help-seeking. They identified clear communication, training, reliable work systems, manageable workloads, regular check-ins, peer connection, wellness resources, and recognition as important forms of support. The findings support practical interventions that combine individual coping resources with organizational measures to promote sustainable remote healthcare work and contribute to nursing administration, occupational health, and digital workforce management.

Developing emotional intelligence (EI) in higher education requires innovative pedagogical approaches supported by objective assessment methods. This study evaluated the effectiveness of an immersive virtual reality (VR) dance intervention for enhancing EI among Chinese university students by integrating motion analysis, physiological measurements, and computational modeling. A randomized controlled trial involving 145 participants was conducted over an eight-week intervention period. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: immersive VR dance training using head-mounted displays, two-dimensional (2D) screen-based dance instruction, or a control group receiving no practical training. Emotional intelligence was assessed using the Mayer–Salovey–Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test (MSCEIT) before the intervention, immediately afterward, and at a four-week follow-up. Motion kinematics, physiological indicators, and computational analyses were integrated to evaluate learning outcomes. In addition, an exploratory algorithmic personalization approach adapted the training protocol to individual participant characteristics. Participants in the VR group demonstrated an average improvement of 18.5 MSCEIT points (Cohen’s d = 1.68) together with a 34.2% increase in movement amplitude. Improvements in the 2D group were substantially smaller (7.3 points; d = 0.51), while the control group showed only minimal gains (2.1 points). The exploratory personalization analysis suggested an additional 23% improvement in intervention effectiveness. At the four-week follow-up, participants retained 76.2% of the acquired gains.

Virtual reality exposure therapy provides a controlled, adjustable method for phobia desensitization, but treatment effectiveness depends on careful calibration of exposure intensity. This study evaluated vibrotactile haptics as a graded design variable in VR phobia treatment, emphasizing dose-response effects across exposure stages. Participants completed repeated VR exposure sessions under four haptic conditions: minimal or no haptics, low-dose feedback, moderate-dose feedback, and high-dose vibrotactile cues. Feedback varied in amplitude, duration, and timing, including event-linked and sustained vibration patterns. Outcomes included fear activation, habituation, progression, early termination, perceived control, presence, workload, and acceptability. Results showed a non-linear dose-response relationship. Moderate feedback produced the strongest therapeutic and usability profile by increasing engagement and fear activation while remaining tolerable enough to support progression and habituation. Higher doses increased realism and arousal but also caused distraction, overload, and greater early-termination risk. Carefully calibrated haptics may therefore strengthen VR phobia treatment across diverse users and stages.
topics: Anxiety, Depression, Psychometrics, Treatment, Cognitive Processes

documents.abstract: Nature-based solutions (NbS) are increasingly used to reduce flood risk and improve water management in flood-prone areas. However, research remains fragmented across disciplines, regions, and scales, making it difficult to identify research trends, knowledge gaps, and priorities. This study presents an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted systematic review of peer-reviewed articles published between 2016 and 2025, retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, a large language model (LLM) was used to screen titles and abstracts, followed by full-text review by the research team. A structured dataset was developed through LLM-assisted data extraction and human validation. Semantic clustering and LLM-assisted synthesis were then used to identify research themes and summarize implementation conditions, benefits, limitations, and research needs. A total of 185 studies were included, which were predominantly published between 2021 and 2025. Nine research themes emerged, with urban green infrastructure for runoff mitigation, spatial planning and decision support, and catchment and hydraulic modeling accounting for 47.6% of the studies. Research was concentrated in the United Kingdom, China, and the United States, with limited representation from Africa and Latin America. The evidence relied mainly on scenario modeling and short monitoring periods, while social equity, public acceptance, and maintenance outcomes were rarely assessed using standardized metrics. While literature reviews have been previously done on the topic of NbS for flood-prone water management, to our knowledge, this is the first review of NbS for flood-prone water management to combine LLM-assisted screening, data extraction, and synthesis with semantic clustering and human validation. The study provides a thematic evidence map, examines temporal and geographic research trends, and presents a reproducible workflow to support future environmental evidence synthesis.

Military airborne training exposes soldiers to high biomechanical loads during parachute landing falls (PLFs), contributing to persistent lower-extremity injury risk. While ankle braces exist that reduce injury, operational adoption is very low. This paper presents a human-centered design case study focused on the development of a wearable sensor sock for assessing PLF biomechanics and supporting training evaluation. Stakeholder engagement, operational site visits, and laboratory testing were used to iteratively refine the wearable system’s sensing strategy, wearability, and integration within existing training workflows. The prototype integrated force sensing resistors, inertial measurement units, strain sensors, and electromyography sensors to measure plantar loading, landing impact characteristics, ankle kinematics, and lower-leg muscle activation patterns relevant to PLF performance. Key lessons learned highlight the importance of designing wearable systems that align with user culture, instructional practice, and the realities of field deployment.

LLM agents are often evaluated by reducing execution traces to labels such as final-answer correctness, tool verification, and fault propagation. These labels are measurements produced by parsers, behavioral detectors, and harness rules, and they may not fully capture what the trace shows. We study this in a tool-use setting built on GSM8K, where agents call a calculator whose outputs are occasionally corrupted, giving clear ground truth for what the tool returned, what the model later used, and what the detectors reported. We audit three trace-level detectors across six production models and 30 problems per model. Final correctness, visible re-verification, and fault propagation can disagree in systematic ways. A key failure mode is silent tool-output override: the calculator returns a corrupted value, but the model later uses a different, often correct, value without calling the tool again, so the bad value stops propagating while a verification detector records no re-check. Human review of 90 traces agrees perfectly with the automated labels for final correctness (67/67), fault impact (19/19), and fault relevance (18/18), but only 67/81 for verification; all 14 disagreements fall into four recurring patterns. Execution limits also change the reported result: in an ablation across two models, one ranges from 21/30 to 27/30 correct as step and token budgets change, while the other stays between 27/30 and 29/30. These findings motivate measurement transparency: an automated label should come with the trace evidence behind it, whether the question the detector asks applied to that trace, whether the run was cut off by an execution limit, and any human corrections. Our trace viewer makes this information inspectable alongside the reported results.

As AI-based decision-support systems become increasingly embedded in physical education and coaching practice, agreement and disagreement between algorithmic advice and participants’ immediate scenario judgments have become important but theoretically underexamined features of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in a shared Judge-Advisor System paradigm, four scenario-based experiments (total N = 859) manipulated whether an experimentally presented AI recommendation was consistent or conflicting with each participant’s prior judgment and tested machine trust and collaborative decision-making self-efficacy as psychological pathways to self-reported collaborative adaptive responses. Psychological resilience and rationale provision were examined as study-specific boundary conditions. Conflict significantly reduced machine trust (Study 1, d = 1.061) and self-efficacy (Study 2, B = −0.687), and both measured mediators carried significant negative indirect associations with adaptive responses (Study 1, B = −0.428; Study 2, via trust B = −0.201, via self-efficacy B = −0.127). Psychological resilience attenuated the between-condition difference in self-efficacy in Study 3 (index of moderated mediation = 0.115). In Study 4, rationale provision moderated the condition-to-trust association, F (1, 239) = 11.348, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.045: the conflict effect was −0.811 in the black-box condition but −0.182 when a rationale was provided. The manipulation therefore concerns advice-judgment agreement rather than a direct experimental comparison of data-driven judgment with established experiential intuition. Because the scenarios did not establish objective recommendation accuracy, the moderation patterns are interpreted as changes in psychological response rather than as evidence that preserving trust or self-efficacy necessarily improves calibration, decision quality, or welfare.

We report a qualitative study spanning more than six months with upper-primary students (ages 9–12) in southern China using a local LLM (Doubao) for writing. Two interview waves with ten students (nine re-interviewed) and six teachers (three re-interviewed) reveal a set of recurring shifts in our focal cohort: from novelty to strategy, from anthropomorphic “companion/virtual teacher” to tool-like framing, and from quick unsticking to guarded use shaped by dependence, fairness, and exam-transfer Footnote1 concerns. Students valued speed and breadth but noted mechanical tone, age/style mismatch, and weak transfer to AI-free tests. We map a Control × Dependency framework and before/after transitions, and surface tensions around classroom norms and equity amid policy ambiguity and uneven AI literacy. We suggest process-visible, agency-preserving integration: sentence- and phrase-level provenance with mandatory micro-edits, task-specific scaffold ceilingsFootnote2, and process-anchored assessment schemes that explicitly factor in AI-use traces.

Purpose The purpose of this study is to present a conceptual model investigating the moderating role of individuals’ ethical positions (idealism and relativism) in the relationship between dependence on artificial intelligence (AI) for decisions and moral disengagement. Design/methodology/approach Theoretical explanations and logical connections among the variables are developed within a propositional framework by integrating conservation of resources theory, social cognitive theory and ethics position theory, informed by research on algorithmic decision-making and moral disengagement. Findings This study proposes that dependence on AI for decisions is positively associated with moral disengagement. Idealism is expected to weaken this relationship, whereas relativism is expected to strengthen it where organisational performance demands favour accepting AI recommendations despite foreseeable stakeholder harm. The model concerns employees who retain meaningful discretion over AI-supported decisions. Practical implications Organisations should provide meaningful opportunities to question and escalate AI recommendations and examine whether performance expectations discourage ethical review. Training should address stakeholder harm and responsibility-displacing rationalisations. Originality/value This study distinguishes dependence on AI for decisions from general AI usage and restrictions on employee autonomy. It develops an explanation of how such dependence may facilitate moral disengagement and identifies idealism and relativism as distinct boundary conditions, specifying the context of the proposed strengthening effect of relativism.

Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

documents.abstract: Introduction Motivation is closely related to students' engagement in learning, yet the associations of intrinsic motivation (IM) and externally oriented motivation (EM) may differ depending on whether they are examined separately or simultaneously. This study examined their shared and unique associations with self-reported creative-process practices (CPP) and learning engagement (LE) among Chinese university art students. Methods Survey data were collected from 481 students enrolled in art programs in one Chinese province using purposive sampling. Confirmatory factor analysis was used to evaluate the four-factor measurement model, followed by structural equation modeling of three specifications: an IM-only model, an EM-only model, and a simultaneous IM-EM model. Results When examined separately, both IM and EM were positively associated with CPP and LE and showed significant indirect associations with LE through CPP. When modeled simultaneously, IM retained significant associations with CPP and LE, whereas the corresponding EM associations and its indirect association through CPP were smaller and no longer statistically significant. The CPP-LE association remained positive and statistically significant across all three model specifications. Discussion The findings indicate that externally oriented motivation can show meaningful associations when considered independently, but much of this association may overlap with intrinsic motivational variance. They also highlight the importance of distinguishing separate from unique motivational associations and of treating creative-process practices and learning engagement as related but conceptually distinct aspects of creative learning.

Generative AI models are capable of generating human-like content, such as large language models (LLMs) generate texts. To automate processes, certain requirements regarding trustworthiness and correctness are fulfilled. To relieve people from controlling the created content, a concept known as LLM-as-a-judge is available. In this scenario, another instance of an LLM is prompted to act as a judge, and check the generated content for certain quality requirements. However, such a judgement might not always align with a human judgement. Besides noise and errors in the human judgement, another reason is just the fact that different human evaluators can have different opinions about the evaluation. One reason could be that there might be no universal or unequivocal assessment since it is challenging to formulate objective rules. This natural existence of variance in human judgement defines the best possible benchmark level of alignment for a model judge. In this work, a method is presented to calculate this best possible benchmark under variance in human judgement. By comparing the distribution of the deviations between human judgement with the distribution of the deviation between model and human judgement with statistical means allows defining a model judge as good enough. Thus, a pragmatic way is provided to decide whether human judgement for a specific task can reliably be automated by a model judge in the quality that we can expect from the corresponding human judges. The code and prompts of the analysis performed are available under https://github.com/Ocean-code-1995/llm-judge-good-enough .

Decision support systems (DSS) are often evaluated before users have much direct experience with them. As a result, the way these systems are labeled may shape selection, reliance, and perceived reliability from the outset. The present work examined whether displayed source and scale labels bias DSS use in a timed object-detection task. Participants searched cluttered images for a bat after choosing between advisors differentiated by source, either human-crowd or machine-generated, and scale, either medium or large. Two experiments were conducted: a default-label (DL) experiment, in which displayed labels matched the underlying recommendation source, and a flipped-label (FL) experiment, in which displayed source labels were decoupled from the underlying source. Overall, source and scale labels affected different stages of DSS use. Participants selected larger-scale labels above chance, while machine-labeled assistance was not selected more often than human-crowd-labeled assistance. Compliance was high and closely matched advisor accuracy, with slightly higher compliance for large-labeled than medium-labeled assistance. Response times mainly reflected repeated exposure. Perceived reliability ratings showed a significant label condition × displayed source interaction, and error-type analyses suggested greater vulnerability to false-positive recommendations under a human-crowd label. Together, these results suggest that source and scale labels shape initial selection, trial-level reliance, and post-use reliability judgments in different ways.

Asked what to study, which career to pursue, or what product to build, large language models (LLMs) often recommend AI-related options. We ask where this tendency comes from by comparing models before and after fine-tuning and by varying how questions are asked. First, pretrained models already include explicit AI/ML terms in the recommendations of 27% of their responses, and their released instruction-tuned versions do so in 59%. Second, fine-tuning models ourselves shows that this rise is not inevitable: general instruction tuning leaves the rate unchanged, but removing the 7% of instruction examples that concern AI cuts it by 14 percentage points, below the level of the pretrained models it starts from. Data rewarding helpfulness raise it by 9 points, while data ranked by the preferences of diverse simulated users lower it by 9. Finally, with models held fixed, asking for the "best" option or for what to do "right now" raises the rate by 8 and 18 points, whereas telling the model it is an AI advisor adds 4. Overall, the tendency starts in pretraining, and what models learn afterward, together with how a question is phrased, decides how strongly it appears.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Personal intelligence systems are taking on increasingly complex everyday tasks, yet repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations, and unwanted outreach can turn capable assistance into interaction burden. Reducing this burden requires agents to remember how users want to be assisted. However, existing memory benchmarks focus on factual recall and personalized answers and rarely test how agents learn and act on interaction preferences. We introduce MemPABench, an interactive environment for on-policy evaluation of memory in personal agents. MemPABench poses long-horizon tasks requiring agents to decide when to clarify, confirm, or act autonomously. Four grounded simulated users hold 14 preferences across work and personal contexts. Their feedback spans 99 sessions over four months, with five event-driven changes per user testing memory updates. We evaluate preference selection, delivered behavior, and sensitivity to context and preference change. Evaluating four memory systems across four LLM backbones, we find that current memory brings limited gains in preference selection. Retrieval-based systems (i.e. Mem0, MemOS, simple RAG) do not outperform No Memory, while File-based memory improves accuracy but applies preferences beyond relevant contexts. Our analysis shows that current memory struggles to retrieve interaction preferences and adapt to preference changes. Even with the correct preference available, overriding the agent's default interaction habits remains challenging. The environment and dataset are available at https://mempabench.com.

There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

The attention-grabbing and memorable nature of visuals makes them a powerful vehicle for spreading hate online. As platforms increasingly reconsider or scale back content moderation efforts, user-centered interventions are gaining importance as complementary governance strategies. While prior research demonstrates the effectiveness of empathy-based textual counter speech, little is known about the role of visual counter speech in mitigating hateful imagery. This preregistered study examines the effectiveness of user-centered interventions against visual hate speech. Using an experimental design (N = 666), we tested four interventions against a no-intervention control condition in response to hateful images targeting transgender persons: (a) empathy-based textual counter speech, (b) AI-generated generic counter images, (c) AI-generated specific counter images replicating elements of the original, and (d) platform-issued warning labels. Results show substantial variation across interventions. Empathy-based textual counter speech and AI-generated specific counter images showed the most consistent reductions in amplification-oriented behaviors, particularly forwarding. Visual interventions did not outperform textual counter speech, suggesting that effectiveness depends less on modality and more on the specificity and contextual alignment of the intervention. Furthermore, effectiveness varied with the intensity of the hate content. Interventions were most effective for humor-based, more ambiguously harmful content, whereas their impact diminished for more severe forms of hate. The consistent performance of AI-generated specific counter images further points to the potential of generative AI to provide users with a rapid, low-cost, and accessible means of producing context-sensitive counter speech.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Employment can finance higher education and generate substantial learning, yet it can also displace study, restrict scholarly participation and expose students to conflicting institutional demands. These different relationships cannot be governed adequately through a single rule on attendance or work experience. This article develops the Rwanda Integrated Work-Study Framework through a structured critical synthesis of regulatory documents, selected institutional provisions, international policy mechanisms and academic literature. A bounded, reproducibly documented search of two academic discovery services returned 50 records; after deduplication and screening, 33 reports were sought and 12 full reports were assessed and retained. Purposefully selected theoretical, policy and recent synthesis sources complemented this corpus. PRISMA-informed reporting records the executed search without claiming an exhaustive systematic review. The analysis identifies a need to distinguish qualification levels, credit volume, approved duration, delivery arrangements and the assessment of workplace learning. Its central contribution is dual assurance: educational support should respond to demonstrated need, whereas academic recognition should depend on independently assessed learning. Regulatory authority and learner protection govern both decisions; credit additionally requires qualification-level equivalence. Six interconnected domains operationalise this distinction across undergraduate, master's and doctoral education. Hypothetical cases expose potential failures involving informal employment, financial hardship, clinical practice and employer-controlled research. The framework offers transparent decision rules, safeguards and evaluation measures rather than evidence of implementation effectiveness. It provides a context-sensitive basis for improving access and recognising workplace learning while retaining academic independence and demanding qualification standards.

Abstract Introduction Clinical placements, where students learn through participation in everyday work, are a central component of many health education programs, including biomedical laboratory science (BLS). While research has primarily focused on students’ experiences, less is known about how participating staff perceive their role. This study explores how BLS staff perceive and enact clinical training. Materials and methods A qualitative study was conducted comprising four focus groups with BLS staff from two hospital settings, including both experienced and newly employed staff. Interviews were analysed using inductive thematic analysis. Activity theory guided a subsequent analysis of workplace learning tensions. Results Six themes were identified, reflecting staff perceptions related to student training: (1) professional pride and ambassador for the field, (2) organisational aspects, (3) interpretations and perceptions of student motivation and engagement, (4) aspects of own motivation and engagement, (5) responses to perceived student engagement and methods to engage students, and (6) confidence in students, students as helpers. Staff expressed a positive commitment to supporting students and fostering professional identity. However, an Activity Theory analysis identified five interconnected tensions related to production, laboratory quality, onboarding of newly hired, division of responsibility, and pedagogical resources. These tensions shaped staffs’ opportunities to involve and support students in clinical work. Discussion Side-by-side training is an integrated and often implicit part of everyday work. Strengthening clinical education requires recognising training as a shared organisational responsibility and creating conditions that support student participation.

Aligned large language models are trained to comply with benign requests while refusing harmful ones. However, recent work shows that this refusal behavior is fragile and can often be disrupted by simple activation- or weight-space interventions. In particular, refusal has been shown to be largely mediated by a single residual-stream direction, typically computed as a difference-of-means vector between harmful and harmless prompts. However, this standard construction aggregates heterogeneous harmful prompts into one uniform average, potentially conflating distinct refusal-related phenomena. In this work, we study whether refusal interventions can be strengthened by learning how to combine prompt-specific refusal directions. We propose Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization (WRDO), a procedure that constructs a composite refusal direction from a bank of per-prompt directions using learned aggregation weights. This approach allows different harmful prompts to contribute unequally to the final intervention direction. We evaluate WRDO against prior single-direction methods on three open-weight language models using three guard judges and HarmBench as an external evaluator. We further measure the effect of the intervention on general model capability through standard utility benchmarks. Finally, we investigate a defense-oriented setting in which the same optimization machinery is used in reverse to restore refusal behavior in an abliterated model checkpoint. Our results show that weighted aggregation provides a more effective and flexible mechanism for manipulating refusal representations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human–robot interaction (HRI) failures remain a major barrier to deploying robots in real-world environments. Prior work often treats failures as isolated technical faults or focuses on post-hoc recovery behaviors. In practice, many breakdowns arise because humans and robots operate under inconsistent assumptions about the current world state. We propose WSM-Aware HRI, an IoT-enhanced modular framework that unifies diverse HRI breakdowns as World-State Mismatches (WSMs) between a human's instruction-implied assumptions and a robot's grounded world model built from multimodal perception and digital augmentation. A Large Language Model (LLM) is used to make implicit assumptions explicit, map them to a small set of mismatch types, and specify the evidence needed for verification against the robot's world state. WSM-Aware HRI shifts failure handling from execution-time recovery to proactive mismatch detection during intention formation, enabling interventions guided by safety, norm compliance, and multi-user coordination with transparent explanations. We evaluate mismatch identification in ten everyday cases spanning both visual and latent-state mismatches. The system can accurately produce the expected output results, and ablations show that reliable identification depends on appropriate grounding representations and verification-oriented refinement. These results indicate that treating interaction breakdowns as explicit world–state mismatches enables earlier detection of impending failures and offers a principled mechanism for integrating external evidence and social constraints into human–robot interaction.

Molecular-genetic analysis of soybean yield and yield components under drought is a crucial element for the development of effective breeding strategies and sustainable agricultural production. The aim of this review is to critically analyse current data from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and identified genetic loci, SNP markers, and candidate genes associated with yield components in soybean in dry conditions with limited water supply and adequate watering (controls). In the results, 346 genetic associations, and 229 candidate genes with KEGG-based potential functions were sufficiently described in published papers and selected for the current study. Three statistically significant metabolic pathways were identified with isoflavonoid biosynthesis, glycosaminoglycan degradation and cysteine and methionine metabolism. The main limitation of the presented analysis was found in the low level of heritability for the studied traits, together with human factors such as carrying out and interpreting GWAS affecting the results presented in the current study. Additionally, complex multigenic controls were reported for the studied traits in soybean and a high level of genotype × environment interactions. Nevertheless, the presented data provide a basis for developing molecular strategies to improve soybean yield in conjunction with better potential drought tolerance.

documents.abstract: Multimodal ocean modeling remains challenging due to substantial heterogeneity in data structures, physical semantics, and spatiotemporal characteristics across satellite imagery, gridded oceanographic fields, and buoy observations. Existing approaches largely focus on task-specific ocean modeling, while learning transferable representations from heterogeneous observations remains an open problem. To address this challenge, we propose YingLan, a multimodal ocean foundation model that integrates physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding, Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC), and ocean-state evolution-aware pretraining. Specifically, the dynamic encoding mechanism generates adaptive input projections conditioned on physical semantics and observation characteristics, enabling flexible representation of heterogeneous ocean variables. STIC models multiscale spatiotemporal dependencies through cross-scale interactions of latent temporal increments. The pretraining strategy further combines masked observation reconstruction with temporal evolution objectives to facilitate the learning of coherent ocean-state representations across different prediction horizons. YingLan is implemented using MindSpore and trained on Huawei Ascend 910B NPUs, demonstrating its compatibility with domestic AI computing infrastructure. In a seven-day sea surface salinity (SSS) forecasting task conducted in the Shenzhen coastal waters, YingLan achieves an average RMSE of 0.687508 PSU, corresponding to relative error reductions of 0.58%, 5.31%, and 12.42% compared with LangYa, XiHe, and GloNet2, respectively. These results provide initial evidence of the model's effectiveness in regional ocean forecasting, while broader cross-task and cross-regional evaluations remain necessary to assess its generalization capabilities.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) are critical infrastructure yet face escalating cyber-physical threats. Traditional intrusion detection systems rely on centralized architectures and implicit trust, which become vulnerabilities in large-scale, adversarial settings. We introduce ZeroTrust-MapAI, a framework that synergizes zero-trust principles, artificial intelligence, and MapReduce to achieve secure and scalable intrusion detection for big-data WSNs. The framework continuously verifies every node and communication, employs distributed autoencoders with Byzantine-robust federated learning, and processes security logs in a MapReduce pipeline. Evaluation on two large-scale datasets yields weighted F1-scores of 0.847 on WSN-DS and 0.826 on EdgeIIoTset, outperforming standard baselines. Under 30% Byzantine attack, ZeroTrust-MapAI maintains strong performance (F1: 0.829– 0.841 across attack types), while FedAvg degrades significantly. The MapReduce pipeline demonstrates effective parallelization with nearlinear speedup up to 8 partitions. This work provides a practical architectural blueprint for building secure, scalable, zero-trust-inspired sensing infrastructures.

The rapid growth of digital banking, instant payments, mobile applications and card-not-present transactions has improved access to financial services while simultaneously widening the attack surface for fraud.Conventional rulebased systems remain indispensable for regulatory control, yet they are often unable to recognize subtle, coordinated and previously unseen patterns.This paper presents a condensed systematic review of artificial intelligence (AI) in banking fraud detection, organised according to the PRISMA 2020 reporting logic.It synthesizes evidence on supervised learning, anomaly detection, deep learning, graph analytics, natural language processing and hybrid decision systems.The review shows that tree-based ensembles generally perform strongly on structured transaction data; sequential neural networks are useful for behavioural histories; graph methods are promising for mule-account and fraud-ring detection; and anomaly models support discovery where labels are scarce.However, accuracy alone is misleading in highly imbalanced datasets.Precision, recall, F1-score, precision-recall area, false-positive cost, detection latency and financial value saved are more meaningful.The review further identifies concept drift, delayed labels, data leakage, limited public datasets, explainability, privacy and bias as major implementation concerns.It concludes that the most credible banking architecture is layered, adaptive and human-supervised rather than dependent on a single algorithm.PRISMA 2020 is used as the reporting framework because it improves transparency in identification, screening, eligibility assessment and synthesis of studies.

ObjectiveEvaluate the sensitivity of eye-tracking metrics to variations in mental workload in rail traffic control, and how they may be modulated by operator experience.BackgroundRail traffic control is a safety-critical domain characterized by high cognitive demands. While subjective workload measures are widely used, objective, real-time indicators, particularly eye-tracking metrics, remain underexplored.MethodEighteen professional rail traffic controllers (9 novice, 9 experienced) performed a simulation-based experiment involving four different scenarios with varying traffic density and task complexity, while wearing a head-mounted eye tracker. Measures of gaze behavior and visual strategies (fixations in different areas of interest (AOI)) were computed, and compared to subjective workload measures, to assess the effects of task difficulty and experience.ResultsSome measures like pupil dilation showed substantial changes (by ∼100%), while others like stationary gaze entropy showed more modest changes (∼40%), with increased task demand. Measures such as fixation rate revealed significant interaction effects with experience, indicating distinct visual strategies of novices vs. experts. Compared to experts, novices relied more on global overview displays under higher workload, and reduced planning-related information use, as revealed by AOI analysis. Subjective workload measures corroborated with increases in perceived demand.ConclusionThis study advances mental workload assessment in rail traffic control by demonstrating that eye-tracking metrics are sensitive to workload variations, and also reveal underlying cognitive strategies unique to expertise.ApplicationThese findings support the development of real-time workload monitoring systems and inform training interventions focused on information integration and cognitive strategies in rail traffic control operations.

Heritage tourism is at a critical inflection point. While access infrastructure has improved considerably over the past two decades, a persistent gap remains between physical access and meaningful participation for visitors with disabilities. This chapter argues that the challenge of inclusive heritage tourism is no longer primarily one of quantity, such as ramps, captioning, or barrier-free entry points, but of quality: of experience, agency, and empowerment. Drawing on a sociotechnical perspective and grounded in the social model of disability, the chapter proposes a three-tiered conceptual framework moving from Access to Inclusion to Empowerment, and examines the role of intelligent, adaptive, and participatory technologies as the infrastructure that can bridge these tiers. Four technology domains are examined in depth: User-governed journey orchestration systems, user-controlled AI travel companions, adaptive multisensory and extended reality (XR) platforms, and co-creative generative AI heritage applications. The chapter concludes with implications for heritage managers, technology developers, and policymakers, and charts a future research agenda centred on governance, dignity, and co-design.

Designing Conversational AI systems to support older adults with MCI necessitates robustness in handling complex and personalized interactions. In this study, we investigate how older adults with MCI experience, navigate and attempt to repair breakdowns while interacting with a voice-based AI system in their homes for medication management through the lens of interactional ”seams”. Through a 20-week in-home deployment with 7 participant dyads, we analyzed 844 interactions to identify interactional and conversational breakdowns and user repair strategies. Drawing on post-deployment interviews, we reflect on the nature of these breakdowns and older adults’ experiences of mitigating them. We further illustrate how older adults draw on their situated knowledge and environment to make sense of and recover from these disruptions, highlighting the cognitive effort required in doing so. Our findings emphasize the collaborative nature of interaction in human-AI contexts, and point to the need for voice assistants to better align with users’ expectations for memory, their routines and external resources in their environment. We conclude by discussing opportunities for voice assistants to integrate contextual knowledge from older adults’ sociotechnical environment and to facilitate more meaningful and user-centered interactions.

The increasing complexity of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and their integration with IT infrastructures has significantly expanded the cyber threat landscape. Traditional cybersecurity models, primarily based on the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA triad), fail to capture the broader societal and operational impacts of cyberattacks. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates Digital Twin technology with a Cyber-Social Security model to simulate, analyze, and quantify cyber threats in critical infrastructures. Virtualized ICS environments built with Mininet and MiniCPS are used to model attack scenarios and assess their consequences across technical and social dimensions. At the core of the framework lies the Cyber-Social Vulnerability Scoring System (CSVSS), a quantitative metric that extends CVSS with a Social Impact dimension grounded in the Entity and Place pillars, producing a single, reproducible severity score that reflects real-world consequences. Crucially, the framework does not automate risk assessment but keeps the human analyst at its center: a Large Language Model (LLM) performs a first-pass analysis, mapping vulnerabilities and drafting risk reports, while the analyst, supported by explainable AI feedback, validates the findings and retains decision authority over critical cases. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's ability to model and score cyber-social impact, while the human-in-the-loop design is presented as a conceptual principle to preserve oversight.

Abstract Introduction: According to the World Health Organization, traffic accidents are a leading cause of fatalities, particularly among young adults aged 5–29, with hemorrhage being the primary cause of death in traumatic incidents. The average time from the onset of shock to death is approximately 2 h, illustrating the need for rapid assessment, timely intervention, and prompt transport to a trauma centre. EEmergency Medical Professional (EMP), are typically the first on the scene to attend to patients with traumatic injuries and play a crucial role in determining patient outcomes; they must be on their toes in the management of these emergencies. Methods: Our aim was to assess the proficiency of Emergency Medical Professionals (EMPs) in handling hemorrhagic shock in a simulated scenario. The simulation study comprised 300 Emergency Medical Professionals, both new and experienced across India, and was conducted over a period of 6 months. The participants were scored on a checklist with a maximum of 10 points. High-fidelity manikins were used, and participants were divided into 30 groups for 45-min sessions, which included pre-briefing, simulation, and debriefing. Results: The results demonstrate strong proficiency among EMPs in initial trauma assessment skills but reveal critical gaps in recognizing life-threatening conditions like exsanguinating hemorrhage and “Load and Go” situations. Despite exhibiting technical proficiency in the International Trauma Life Support ITLS primary survey, participants struggled to translate assessments into life-saving interventions. There was a significant failure to recognize exsanguinating hemorrhage (46.7%), declare “load-and-go” situations (36.3%), and administer tranexamic acid (0%). In the Indian context of prolonged transport times, this lack of situational awareness is concerning. Bridging this gap requires targeted, simulation-based experiential learning to help EMPs evolve from simply completing checklists to executing rapid, critical prioritization in real-world emergencies. Conclusion: The study highlights a notable proficiency gap among EMPs in key shock management skills, emphasizing the importance of continuous training to enhance patient outcomes and elevate care standards in trauma care.

Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) can progress rapidly to end-stage liver disease without timely remission. Interpatient heterogeneity and severe presentations often preclude standard immunosuppression, increasing early clinical deterioration in hospitalized patients even with standard care. We developed and independently validated a machine-learning model to predict treatment failure risk upon admission. We conducted a dual-cohort study comprising a retrospective discovery cohort (n = 314, 2017–2025) and a consecutive temporal validation cohort (n = 66, 2025–2026). Following ensemble-based feature selection, 13 machine-learning algorithms were evaluated. The optimal model was interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and benchmarked against the conventional Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) and Child-Pugh score. Seven predictors were identified: alanine aminotransferase (ALT), total bile acid (TBA), Child-Pugh score, immunoglobulin M (IgM), total bilirubin (TBil), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). The Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) achieved superior discrimination (AUC = 0.762), significantly outperforming MELD (AUC = 0.555) and Child-Pugh (AUC = 0.611) scores, with satisfactory calibration and clinical utility. Predictive efficacy was maintained in the temporal validation cohort (AUC = 0.755). SHAP analysis revealed a dual biological trade-off: pronounced inflammatory activity (elevated ALT) inversely correlated with treatment failure risk, whereas severe cholestasis and impaired hepatic reserve drove adverse outcomes. This non-invasive GBM model quantifies the complex clinical interplay among active inflammation, cholestatic severity, and depleted hepatic reserve. Overcoming limitations of static scoring systems, it provides a reliable, actionable tool for personalized risk stratification and preemptive therapeutic decision-making in heterogeneous AIH patients upon index admission. When patients are hospitalized for autoimmune hepatitis, it is often difficult for doctors to predict who will worsen despite receiving standard treatments. We developed an artificial intelligence tool that uses routine blood tests to calculate a patient’s risk of treatment failure the moment they are admitted to the hospital. This early warning system allows doctors to quickly identify high-risk patients and personalize their care with more effective or intensive therapies right from the start.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence moves beyond answering questions and begins acting on our behalf, institutions face two connected problems. People may retain formal authority while losing the practical conditions needed to exercise judgment. Meanwhile, AI systems can carry out technically correct actions without legitimate authorization. This manifesto argues for human agency, legitimate institutional authority, and accountable action. It examines meaningful human oversight, the limits of delegated authority, verification when actions produce consequences, and the obligations of those who govern AI. Its guiding principle, Authority Before Autonomy, calls for responsible delegation without surrendering the capacity to question, correct, and answer for what follows.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The oral route remains the most preferred route for drug administration due to its ease and patient acceptance, but conventional dosage forms require frequent dosing which leads to fluctuations in plasma drug levels. To overcome this problem, sustained release matrix tablets have been developed as an effective alternative. In this system, the drug is uniformly dispersed within a polymer matrix that controls its release over an extended period of time. Various types of polymers such as hydrophilic polymers like hydroxypropyl methylcellulose, hydrophobic polymers like ethyl cellulose and natural polymers like xanthan gum and guar gum are used as release retardants. The release of drug from matrix tablet takes place mainly by diffusion through gel layer, swelling of polymer and slow erosion of matrix. Recently, the field has witnessed remarkable innovations including blending of natural and synthetic polymers, introduction of gastro-retentive and mucoadhesive matrix systems, application of 3D printing for personalized tablets and development of pH sensitive smart matrices. These advancements have improved the efficiency and safety of matrix systems. Looking ahead, the combination of biodegradable polymers, nanocarriers and artificial intelligence based design is expected to make matrix tablets more targeted, sustainable and patient friendly. This review summarizes the current status, release mechanisms, recent developments and future scope of matrix tablets for sustained drug delivery.

documents.abstract: Knowledge graph construction typically involves data preprocessing, entity recognition, relation extraction, knowledge fusion, conflict resolution, and quality assessment. However, heterogeneous documents in substation operation and maintenance (O&M), including technical standards, defect records, work tickets, operational logs, and scanned or mixed-format documents, exhibit dense domain terminology, inconsistent expressions, cross-source conflicts, and incomplete provenance, which make accurate and traceable knowledge construction challenging. Existing large-language-model-based and pipeline-based methods have improved automatic knowledge extraction, but their processing stages are usually weakly coupled, making it difficult to reuse cross-stage evidence, trace downstream errors to responsible upstream tasks, and perform targeted rework. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a shared-task-state-driven multi-agent collaborative knowledge graph construction framework (MAC-CKG). The framework introduces a task orchestrator and a shared task-state pool to coordinate five agents for data processing, entity recognition, relation extraction, knowledge fusion, and quality assessment; provenance, confidence, conflict, and review information are preserved across stages, while ontology constraints, multifactor confidence, and the two-threshold quality-routing mechanism jointly support knowledge insertion, human review, and targeted rework. For evaluation, we constructed a heterogeneous substation O&M dataset comprising 96 heterogeneous source items (including documents and structured knowledge resources) and 17,220 standardized input units, yielding a provenance-verified candidate subset of 9519 entities and 9258 relations. An independently annotated 20-document end-to-end benchmark was separately used for raw-document extraction evaluation. Across three independent runs on this benchmark, MAC-CKG achieves mean entity, conditional relation, and strict triple F1 scores of 85.96%, 62.50%, and 62.31%, respectively, outperforming SAC-KG by 2.83, 5.77, and 6.34 percentage points and PiVe by 4.48, 8.32, and 8.94 percentage points. Independent-benchmark ablation further reduces triple F1 from 62.31% to 59.68% without task orchestration and to 57.41% without the shared task-state pool, showing sensitivity to these components under the evaluated configurations, with inference cost considered separately.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being considered for Human Resource Management (HRM), including recruitment, employee selection, training and development, performance management, employee engagement, and workforce planning. This paper reviews the applications, potential benefits, challenges, and ethical considerations associated with AI in HRM. The study follows a descriptive approach based on secondary sources, including academic literature and professional reports. The review suggests that AI may support routine tasks, organize workforce information, and assist HR decisionmaking. However, privacy, algorithmic bias, implementation costs, accuracy, technical knowledge, and employee trust remain important concerns. The paper concludes that AI should support rather than replace human judgement, with responsible policies, data protection, and appropriate human supervision.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has historically diverged into class-aware methods, which highlight discriminative regions for specific target classes, and class-agnostic methods, which capture dominant feature representations regardless of the classification outcome. In this paper, we introduce a unified attribution framework that bridges this gap by explicitly separating the attribution target from the feature extraction operator. Specifically, we project deep activations onto multiple dominant principal components to extract robust, class-agnostic structural maps, while utilizing class-aware gradients to localize target-specific semantics. To synthesize these complementary perspectives, we propose a logit-margin-based fusion mechanism that shifts attribution priority based on the model’s predictive margin. We evaluate our framework in a cross-domain zero-shot setting by applying ImageNet-pretrained architectures (ResNet-50, DenseNet-121) to the Oxford-IIIT Pet dataset. Our zero-shot evaluation shows that the proposed fusion provides an alternative combination of class-aware and class-agnostic evidence. The results suggest that adaptively combining feature-level representation maps with target-driven discriminative maps offers a distinct tool for interpreting CNN representations across domain shifts.

This documentary essay examines how political, military, environmental, and public-health crises are deliberately produced, amplified, or exploited, and how their consequences may shape governance on the road to 2030. Drawing on institutional records, declassified archives, scientific and humanitarian assessments, contemporary reporting, and the author’s earlier writings, it analyses developments from June 2025 to 20 October 2026 through a critical historical and biblical lens. Cases involving political unrest, Ukraine, Sudan, the Israel–Iran confrontation, natural hazards, and disease emergencies reveal distinct but interacting pathways of intentional harm, institutional opportunism, and social vulnerability. Historical records of covert intervention establish that certain forms of manipulation are real; they do not substantiate a single hidden command directing every contemporary disaster. Public agendas for international coordination, digital identity, artificial intelligence, and financial interoperability likewise create opportunities for cooperation alongside risks of surveillance, exclusion, and concentrated power. The essay evaluates the unverified letter attributed to Albert Pike, the biblical accounts of Isaac and Ishmael, and Persia’s appearance in Ezekiel 38–39 without equating contested claims or eschatological interpretations with historical proof. It also considers military adaptation during the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts while distinguishing operational learning from a predetermined world-war strategy. Retrospective comparison with the author’s pre-2025 warnings identifies thematic continuities but no verified prophetic timetable. A four-part framework distinguishes direct orchestration, organized amplification, opportunistic exploitation, and structural convergence. The essay concludes that Christian preparedness requires biblical fidelity, evidence-based discernment, institutional accountability, compassion for victims, and watchfulness without date-setting.

With the widespread deployment of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in smart grids, visual inspection based on deep learning has significantly advanced. However, conventional object detection paradigms heavily rely on massive, high-quality annotated datasets, struggling with poor generalization and a fundamental “data-hungry” dilemma caused by the extreme scarcity of long-tail defect samples. To overcome these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel zero-shot multimodal agent framework driven by large language models (LLMs). Adopting a centralized star topology, the architecture strictly decouples physical visual perception from high-level business cognition, utilizing an LLM as the cognitive hub and a vision-language model (VLM) as the perception tool. Crucially, the system introduces a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mechanism to dynamically align visual findings with authoritative grid regulations, supporting rule-referenced report generation. Experimental results demonstrate that, without any domain-specific fine-tuning, the proposed framework reduces false alarms under the tested configuration, with a detection F1 score of 82.52%. In a common-report comparison repeated three times, the framework achieves 65.30% correct reference-clause coverage, compared with 43.84% for a direct Qwen-VL-Max call supplied with the same visual priors and rules. The framework extends visual detection to structured, human-readable reports linked to supplied industrial rules; its grading accuracy and repeatability remain dependent on the visual observations and subsequent tool execution.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Purpose Universities are increasingly adopting institutional policies on academic integrity (AcI) and artificial intelligence (AI), but it remains unclear whether these expectations are translated coherently into the course-level documents that govern students’ learning and assessment. This article therefore examines how AcI and AI, including generative AI (GenAI), are articulated in official teaching guides for Spain’s Master’s Degree in Teacher Training, and whether guidance is embedded coherently across course design. Design/methodology/approach A documentary content analysis was conducted on 254 publicly available guides from 68 universities. Explicit AcI and AI references were coded across objectives, competencies, learning outcomes, activities and assessment. Two formative diagnostic indices measured breadth of coverage across these five sections. Mann–Whitney tests compared university and subject types; 25% of the corpus was independently double-coded. Findings AcI was mentioned in 53.5% of guides but was concentrated in assessment and competencies; 46.5% contained no valid reference. Explicit AI guidance remained marginal (6.3%) and primarily assessment-centred. Private universities showed slightly broader AcI coverage, public universities slightly broader AI coverage and Final Master’s Project guides substantially broader AcI coverage. Research limitations/implications The indices measure documentary breadth, not the quality, depth or implementation of guidance, and guides are nested within universities. Practical implications Programme leaders should integrate task-specific integrity and AI expectations across outcomes, activities, assessment, disclosure and formative support, with attention to future teachers’ professional AI literacy. Originality/value The study provides a large-scale, programme-specific audit and a transparent method for benchmarking cross-sectional curricular integration without treating document coverage as a quality score.

When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human-centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH-Research-Lab/AuthorizationBench .

The registration reproduces that protocol; deviations from it are disclosed in the attached document and in the corresponding fields. Systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies comparing the sense of agency (implicit: intentional/temporal binding; explicit: judgments of agency, control and authorship) when adults act or decide together with an artificial agent (robot, autonomous virtual agent, computer partner, AI advisor, chatbot/LLM) versus acting alone or with a human partner. Authors: Martina Nicole Modesti, Antonio Del Casale, Stefano Ferracuti (Sapienza University of Rome).

Pathology foundation models (PFMs) support a wide range of histopathology tasks on whole-slide images through multiple instance learning (MIL). Despite recent progress, these models remain sensitive to cross-hospital distribution shifts: performance often degrades when a task head (e.g., classification) is trained on data from one hospital and then used on data from another hospital. To address this challenge, we propose AdaptMIL, a training strategy for integrating domain adaptation into MIL training. AdaptMIL is motivated by our finding that directly applying domain adaptation objectives during MIL training can interfere with MIL aggregation learning, often resulting in performance degradation over standard training. AdaptMIL resolves this by decoupling representation-level domain alignment learning from MIL aggregation learning through a two-stage training procedure. We show that AdaptMIL improves cross-hospital performance and outperforms alternative adaptation methods across experiments spanning multiple WSI datasets, tasks, PFMs, MIL architectures, and domain adaptation objectives. AdaptMIL's code will be released upon publication.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major public health risk. Testing antimicrobial susceptibility in patients using conventional methods takes a week or more to deliver results, advances in artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL), have created an opportunity to predict AMR with speed by combining data from different sources such as genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, phenotypic, and clinical information. Recent advances in whole genome sequencing, metagenomic methods, and MALDI-TOF mass spectroscopy, as well as the availability of established and curated databases such as the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), are essential components of developing robust models for predicting AMR. A large number of studies using ML and DL methods have demonstrated that they can identify resistance genes, discover new AMR determinants, predict trends in AMR, and improve antimicrobial stewardship and drug discovery. This review describes methodologies currently used to predict AMR with a focus on the types of data used, feature engineering methods, and algorithms used in pathogen-specific and pan-species studies. It discusses several current challenges associated with building predictive models including lack of diversity of datasets, class imbalance, inconsistent methods of testing, limited ability to interpret results, and the need for further validation. Future directions involve developing explainable AI models, federated learning approaches to improve datasets, and integrating digital diagnostics into electronic health records. In conclusion, ML and DL have the potential to revolutionize precision medicine, enhance AMR monitoring, and accelerate the pace of drug development.

The shift to agentic AI represents a major paradigm change in the field of intelligent systems research and development, as these systems are capable of establishing sub-goals, planning for a goal, and executing plans with only minimal human oversight. This capability offers a unique chance to promote gender equality, inclusive digital engagement, and sustainable growth via evolving, accessible and fair AI-based methods throughout industries. Meanwhile, the increased autonomy of agentic AI systems presents unique challenges such as the potential for algorithmic bias to be amplified, decision-making disparities, and a lack of governance, each of which requires responsible AI, transparent governance, and clear ethical frameworks. This paper presents a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis of a 41 paper corpus from Scopus. The review follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines and summarizes the evidence regarding agentic and generative AI architectures, typologies of bias, and sectoral applications in healthcare, education, and gender equity. The paper presents a human-centred conceptual framework for responsible governance of agentic AI, building on lifecycle-governance and equity-by-design approaches, which merges bias mitigation, gender-inclusive design, and sustainability transition. The network of co-authorship is highly fragmented (density = 0.021; number of components = 37 from 88 authors), suggesting that there is no coordinated research agenda and giving empirical support to the integrative framework proposed here. This fragmentation further indicates that the vision and capabilities of agentic AI to contribute to gender equality and education are still not fully explored in the context of governance and sustainability, highlighting the relevance of the framework introduced in this paper. This is a collection of AI topics, derived from the title, that are examined from a gender equality perspective.This is a list of AI keywords that have been explored through the lens of gender equity, based on the title.
